title: Expressing thoughts and actions
summary: Saying what you think with tila, sa akalà, sa palagáy and isip, and saying where you go and what you did with pumuntá and other verbs
goals: Use tila (it seems) at the start of a sentence
Give an opinion with sa akalà ko and sa palagáy ko
Know the difference in feeling between sa akalà and sa palagáy
Use umisip, mag-isíp and isípin for real thinking
Use pumuntá for going to a place, and the plain verb for go swimming, go to sleep

sections.title: Three ways to say I think

blocks.t: When Filipinos express their thoughts and actions, they use the words **tila**, **akalà** and **isip**, which all simply mean *to think* in English. For actions they use **pumuntá** (*to go*) and many other verbs to say what they **did**, **are doing** and **will do**.

The English *to think* can be translated in **three ways**. All three show opinions, ideas and assumptions, and in a sentence they all mean much the same: *I think, he/she thinks, they/we think*. On their own, though, each has its own meaning:

head: Word
What it is
Meaning
blocks.title: Tila, sa akalà and sa palagáy
Two patterns
blocks.note: Tila + a verb, an adjective or a nominative pronoun such as silá or ikáw. Sa + akalà or palagáy + a possessive noun or pronoun.

head: Owner word
Meaning
blocks.title: Possessive words that can follow sa akalà / sa palagáy
blocks.note: These are the possessive forms from Lesson 8.

blocks.t: **Tila** is mostly placed at the **beginning of a sentence** in everyday conversation. It always shows the **speaker's own perception**: this is how things look to me.

items.en: It seems it will rain.

items.tl: Ang sagot niyá ay tila mali.
items.en: His/her answer seems wrong.
She seems prettier now.

sections.title: Sa akalà and sa palagáy: to my thinking

blocks.t: **Sa akalà** and **sa palagáy** are followed by a **noun or pronoun in the possessive form**, such as **ni Coi**, **niyá** or **mo**. The book gives a literal translation (*to my thinking*) and a natural one (*I think*).

items.tl: Sa akalà ko ikaw ay matalíno.
items.en: To my thinking, you are an intelligent man. (literal) I think you are an intelligent man.

items.tl: Sa palagáy ko ay mananálo tayo.
items.en: To my thinking, we will win. (literal) I think we will win.

items.tl: Sa akalà nila, siyá'y may sakít.
items.en: To their thinking, he is sick. (literal) They think he is sick.

items.tl: Sa palagáy ni Gem ay tama ako.
items.en: To Gem's thinking, I am right. (literal) Gem thinks I am right.

head: Phrase
What it suggests to a Tagalog speaker
rows: An **assumption** that may be proven wrong. It leaves room for someone to agree or disagree.

blocks.t: Because of this, **Sa akalà ko ikaw ay matalíno** can mean *I thought you were intelligent*, which somehow takes away from the person's intelligence as the speaker saw it. In the same way, **Akalà ko Amerikáno siyá** (*I thought he is an American*) cancels an earlier assumption.
Tagalog speakers sometimes **leave out sa** before akalà, **replace sa with ang**, and **leave out the linking word ay**. These shorter sentences are still correct:

items.tl: Sa akalà ko ay Amerikáno siyá.
items.en: To my thinking, he is an American.
To my thinking, he is an American.
My assumption is that he is an American.

blocks.title: In my view
blocks.t: An informal way to say *to think*, close to **sa palagáy [ko]**, is **sa tingín [ko]**, which roughly means *in [my] view*.

When *to think* means **to do some real thinking** or **to ponder over something**, Tagalog uses **umisip** or **mag-isíp** (active forms) or **isípin** (passive form). You met -um-, mag- and -in verbs in Lessons 14 and 15.

items.tl: Umiísip siyá ng lálong mabúting paraán.
items.en: He is thinking of a better way.

items.tl: Iniísip niyá ang kanyáng mga sinásabi.
items.en: She thinks about what she says.
(You) Think of what can be done.

blocks.title: Active and passive
items: **Umiísip siyá** (active): the doer siyá is the subject.
**Iniísip niyá** (passive): the doer becomes niyá, and the thing thought about takes **ang**.

sections.title: Pumuntá: to go to a place

blocks.t: To simply show **direction** or where someone is going, **pumuntá** is the exact translation of *to go*. It can also mean **to come**, as in the first example below. Used this way, pumuntá has an **imperative form** and all the tenses of the **-um-** and **mag-** forms.

items.en: Come here. (imperative)
Go there. (imperative)
We will go to church. (future)
They went to the beach. (past)
He/She goes to Manila everyday. (present)

head: Tense
Form
blocks.title: The forms of pumuntá in the examples

blocks.t: English also uses *go* in front of another verb: *went swimming*, *will go to sleep*. Tagalog has **no exact translation** for this. Instead, it uses the **second verb only**, in the right tense or in the imperative.

blocks.title: No auxiliary go
blocks.t: Tagalog does **not** really use pumuntá together with another verb the way English uses *to go* as a helper verb. The English sentence shows the tense on *go*; the Tagalog sentence shows the tense on the main verb only.
Sentences like these are the usual answers to questions such as:

head: Question
Meaning
blocks.title: What did / are / will you do?

items.en: You go to walk (or You walk). (imperative)
We will go swimming. (future)
We went to visit a friend. (past)
They are sleeping in the next room. (present)

blocks.title: Remember
items: Tila (it seems) usually starts a sentence and shows the speaker's own perception.
Sa akalà / sa palagáy + a possessive: sa akalà ko, sa palagáy ni Gem.
Sa akalà is an assumption that may be wrong; sa palagáy is a personal opinion. Informal: sa tingín ko.
Pumuntá = go to a place (also come). For go + verb, use the second verb alone: lumangóy, matutulog.

exercises.q: Which word is an adverb meaning "it seems"?
exercises.explain: Tila = it seems.

exercises.q: Where is tila mostly placed in everyday conversation?
options: At the beginning of the sentence
At the end of the sentence
exercises.answer: At the beginning of the sentence
exercises.explain: Tila úulan. It seems it will rain.

exercises.q: Tila always shows…
exercises.explain: Tila is how things seem to the speaker.

exercises.q: What follows sa akalà or sa palagáy?
options: a nominative pronoun such as ikáw
exercises.explain: Sa akalà ko, sa palagáy ni Gem.

exercises.q: Fill in: Sa palagáy ___ ay mananálo tayo. (I think we will win.)
exercises.explain: Ko is the possessive form needed after palagáy.

exercises.q: Fill in: Sa palagáy ___ Gem ay tama ako. (Gem thinks I am right.)
exercises.explain: Ni goes before a name in the possessive.

exercises.q: "Sa akalà nila, siyá'y may sakít" means…
options: It seems he will be sick.
exercises.explain: Nila = their: to their thinking.

exercises.q: Which phrase leaves room for the assumption to be proven wrong?
exercises.explain: Sa akalà is an assumption; sa palagáy is a personal opinion.

exercises.q: "Akalà ko Amerikáno siyá" is best understood as…
options: I thought he is an American.
He thinks I am an American.
He seems to be an American.
exercises.answer: I thought he is an American.
exercises.explain: It cancels a previous assumption.

exercises.q: "Ang akalà ko Amerikáno siyá" means…
options: My assumption is that he is an American.
exercises.answer: My assumption is that he is an American.
exercises.explain: Sa is replaced by ang, and ay is left out.

exercises.q: Which informal phrase is similar to sa palagáy ko?
exercises.explain: Sa tingín ko roughly means in my view.

exercises.q: Which is the passive form of "to think"?
exercises.explain: Umisip and mag-isíp are active; isípin is passive.

exercises.q: "Mag-isíp ka ng magagawâ" means…
options: (You) Think of what can be done.
He is thinking of a better way.
She thinks about what she says.
exercises.answer: (You) Think of what can be done.
exercises.explain: Mag-isíp ka is an order.

exercises.q: "Pumuntá ka díto" means…
exercises.explain: Pumuntá can also mean to come.

exercises.q: Fill in: ___ kamí sa simbáhan. (We will go to church.)
exercises.explain: Pupuntá is the future.

exercises.q: Fill in: ___ siyá sa Mayníla áraw-áraw. (He/She goes to Manila everyday.)
exercises.explain: Pumupuntá is the present.

exercises.q: How does Tagalog say "went swimming"?
exercises.explain: Only the second verb is used, in the right tense.

exercises.q: How does Tagalog say "will go to sleep"?
exercises.explain: Tagalog does not use pumuntá as a helper verb.

exercises.q: "Anó ang gágawin mo?" means…
exercises.explain: Gágawin is the future.
Pumuntá silá sa tabíng-dágat.
Sa palagáy ko ay mananálo tayo.
Umiísip siyá ng lálong mabúting paraán.
Tila = it seems.

exercises.tl: Sa palagáy ko ay mananálo tayo.
Ang sagot niyá ay tila mali.

exercises.en: We went to visit a friend.
He is thinking of a better way.
exercises.tl: Umiísip siyá ng lálong mabúting paraán.

recap: Tila (it seems) usually starts a sentence: Tila úulan.
Sa akalà / sa palagáy + a possessive word = I think, he thinks…: Sa palagáy ko ay mananálo tayo.
Sa akalà is an assumption that may be wrong; sa palagáy is a personal opinion; sa tingín ko = in my view.
Real thinking: umisip or mag-isíp (active), isípin (passive).
Pumuntá = to go (or come) to a place: pumuntá, pumupuntá, pupuntá.
Go + verb uses the second verb only: Lalangóy kamí. We will go swimming.
